name: Memory Models & Happens-Before
tagline: Constraining compiler reordering and CPU store buffers using formal happens-before edges across x86 TSO and ARM64.
purpose: Understand why code that passes on x86-64 can corrupt state on ARM64, and how acquire/release and seq_cst establish cross-thread visibility.

spark.summary: A memory model defines the exact rules under which writes by one CPU core become visible to another, using a formal partial order called happens-before to constrain compiler reordering, CPU store buffers, and out-of-order execution.
spark.keyTakeaway: If lock contention or cache misses stall worker threads, cache coherence (MESI) guarantees cores eventually agree on a single address, not the order of writes across different addresses—only explicit happens-before edges (mutexes, acquire/release, seq_cst) guarantee cross-thread visibility.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Happens-before ($A \to_{hb} B$)** is a transitive partial order guaranteeing that all memory effects of $A$ are visible to $B$. Within a single thread, program order gives happens-before.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Release-Acquire Handoff Establishing Cross-Thread Visibility (Writer Core -> Store Buffer / L1 -> Atomic Flag -> Reader Core); C++/Rust Atomic Memory Ordering Spectrum (RELAXED -> ACQ / REL -> SEQ_CST).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Each ordering trades fence latency for stronger cross-variable guarantees. Because x86 CI runners hide ARM64 reordering bugs, production systems teams run **ThreadSanitizer (TSan)** in C++/Go, **jcstress** on the JVM, and **Loom** model checking in Rust.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Apply happens-before rules to double-checked locking, JVM escape analysis, and lock-free atomics.

learningJourney.title: Why x86 TSO hides bugs that crash on ARM64

explanation.foundation: Compilers (`-O2`/`-O3`) and CPUs reorder independent loads/stores to hide 50–100 ns DRAM latency. **x86-64 (Total Store Order)** preserves Store-Store and Load-Load order automatically, only allowing Store-Load reordering (Dekker's anomaly).
explanation.core: **ARMv8/ARM64 (Graviton, Apple Silicon)** has a weak memory model allowing Load-Load and Store-Store reordering—so missing `acquire`/`release` fences that 'worked on my x86 laptop' silently read half-initialized structs in production.
